utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. There's one matter to discuss before we hear evidence of Mr. Kezunovic. We note that, Mr. Robinson, the accused has filed his 51st motion on disclosure violation. With respect to that motion, I wonder whether you can identify, with more specificity, the volume of material which the accused will have to review which he contends to pertain to the testimony of Nebojsa Ristic, and how much time he actually needs to review that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The two interviews which were disclosed to us just recently involve one transcript of the interview of Vlatko Lopatic, and from memory, I'm estimating that transcript is about 60 to 80 pages. I think it would take him one to one and a half hours to review that transcript. The second matter that was not disclosed to us until recently was an interview of Dusko Mihajlovic, which was not transcribed, and I, myself, listened to the video of that interview, and it's about four and a half hours. I don't think that Dr. Karadzic would necessarily have to listen to that whole interview. I could point him to the portions of it that are useful for his cross-examination. So I think we could safely say that this whole exercise maybe could be completed within two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger, I wonder whether you can respond orally to this motion by the end of today's hearing, so far as it relates to the requested postponement of Mr. Ristic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will be filing a written submission imminently. I expect it to be filed this morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well, we can proceed. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about another bit of information that was part of the report from the meeting that you attended, and I'm referring to 65 ter 11241. I also believe that it has a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2761, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have page 38 in Serbian and 28 in English. And that's item 4, "Organisation, Staffing and Posts." Could we then have item 4 in English. I think that's the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this: We can -- if we look at the first page, we'll see that this report covers the period from April to December 1991. Now, would you take a look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: April to December 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The paragraph on the personnel policies. Now, are you aware of this information that was provided in the meeting that 210 employees were dismissed over these couple of months, criminal reports were brought against 29, and 59 were suspended?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have D447, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us identify this document together. Its title is "Brief Analysis of the Functioning of the MUP So Far," and it is dated the 11th of July, 1992. Can we have the next page, please. That's page 2 in both the English and Serbian versions. Can you see your name listed here as one of the participants of the meeting? That's in the second paragraph, about the sixth or seventh line from the top.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you did attend this meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have page 8 in both Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we take a look at the bottom, we see that there is a paragraph -- or a bullet point beginning with: "The functional communications system has been destroyed. There have been talks with representatives of Rudi Cajevec ..." And so on and so forth. Now, can you see at the top it says that the army and the crisis are requesting that as many as possible of the Muslims be gathered, and do you recall that there was talk about Trnopolje and other centres where civilians were being evacuated from the areas that were under combat, and they were referred to the police who were guarding them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT REPORTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing no interpretation. Mr. Kezunovic, could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I'm not very familiar with those problems. I don't know any details about that, and I cannot give you a precise response to this question. I really don't recall enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, is it correct that there was an attempt to improvise production, and was this done because there were sanctions imposed and you could not obtain spare parts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was the only source where we could get them from, other than the equipment that we found on the premises. There was nothing else, and the only chance was to work together with Cajevec because they also produced, among other things, the shortwave radio sets and also equipment -- encoding equipment. So they were of a lot of interest to us, as the manufacturer of such products.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have page 2 in both English and Serbian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Page 12, interpreter's correction, of both English and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Mr. Savic and what he has to say. He's from Trebinje, and he says -- or, rather, do you agree that Eastern Herzegovina is bordering on Old Herzegovina; in other words, Gacko and Foca are about 40 kilometres apart, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does he say here that he's unable to provide any information on Stara Herzegovina or Old Herzegovina because the communications are down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, for the time in question there was a total breakdown in communications.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 13 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantic reports here on the situation in Bijeljina. He is the police station commander, but he also mentioned Brcko, and he says, among other things, members of the Red Berets have conducted two attacks -- have carried out two attacks on the Brcko Police Station, but they were disarmed subsequently. Do you remember that there was a lot of talk about many people putting red berets on their heads and then declaring themselves to be Red Berets, and then they would attack our own police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. This was not the only incident of that sort. I believe that such incidents were recorded everywhere. Some were more intense and others less -- of lesser intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We both have to make pauses between question and answer. Could we now have pages 16 in Serbian and 15 in English, please. On the previous page, if we can just see it briefly, we see that these are the words of Minister Stanisic. Can we just show briefly the previous page, just to show who the speaker is. So is this correct; these are the words of Mico Stanisic? You can see it in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it says that: "We must provide the maximum, with minimum efforts. There is a lot demanded of too few people." And then it goes on to say: "At the government levels and in the Presidency, there is constant talk about the need to stop the plundering, to maintain public law and order, provide for the security of civilians ...," et cetera. Do you recall that was the position taken by the minister?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and this was a constant topic with the police officers, whoever attended the meetings, because that was within their scope of work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have page 16 of the English, please, and 17 in Serbian. The third paragraph in Serbian from the top, and in English, I believe that's the paragraph beginning: "We have opted ..." "In order to establish power," and so on, it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we see here that even the MUP has decided to prevent and discover criminal acts perpetrated by military personnel, not just civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. This was an ongoing fight with the army, whether the police could actually take measures against army personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we see here that Vlasto Kusmuk is the next speaker. Can we have the next page in the Serbian, and I believe the same is the case in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third bullet, where he says that the codes have to be determined for each station, and that an encoding system should be set up, and that this issue had not been resolved even as late as the end of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The matter here that he mentioned, the encoding books and the codes, that matter had not been resolved through the very end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page now in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see that the next speaker is Zdravko Borovcanin, and in Serbian, we can stay on the same page. In the next paragraph, he says -- he put the question of jurisdiction to those present, between the army and the MUP, and then the police and paramilitary units. And: "What are we to do about the Muslims who wish to move to another country ...," and so on and so forth. And then in the last paragraph, he says: "He stressed that it was necessary that those who are engaged in criminal activities be removed from among us." Do you recall that he, too, was a proponent of this and that this was actually something that everyone -- the position that everyone took?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I recall that there was a question put to me during one of the interviews - either with the Prosecutor or with the Defence, I can't recall - relating to these very matters, whether that was correct, whether there were any measures taken against such people. And I said then, Believe me, if at any time I learned -- had I at any time learned that the MUP condoned such conduct, I would have left the ministry on that very spot. I wouldn't stay there for another moment, because I cannot recall that anyone condoned such acts. Quite the contrary, everyone tried their best to prevent these things. However, it was general chaos, it was wartime. People just put on uniforms of all colour and kind, and they did whatever they pleased.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see the next page and where we see that the speaker is Dobro Planojevic, assistant minister for crime prevention. In English, that would be on page 19, and in Serbian, page 20. In English, we can see that the speaker is Planojevic. Can we have the next page in Serbian now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The fifth bullet from the top says: "Measures should be taken for our members to know what to waste them in case they commit a crime." And then we should skip one, and the one after that says: "The documenting of war crimes is a priority, and along with documentation (on-site investigation reports, photographs, expert opinions, medical reports) it is necessary to compile lists of war criminals which are to be exchanged with other centres," so that they can be monitored. Do you recall this was Planojevic's position and that it was shared with the other members of the leadership?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I can tell you, when speaking about Dobro Planojevic, that he was one of those who fought such incidents or who was against these. He was, as far as I can recall, one of the most honest people in that respect, because he fought this as hard as he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we -- can it be said, Mr. Kezunovic, of our police system, that, in fact, it was a system that was organised and had a small head, but a huge body, that this small head was supposed to control this huge body? There were few of you, few commanders in various administrations and stations, but the huge problem?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, take a look at what Cedo Kljajic says. He's the under-secretary for public security, and he emphasised the need to document war crimes in order to press criminal charges. Do you know, Mr. Kezunovic, that in Krajina, for instance, all of these processes that were conducted in Bihac and other areas, that are being conducted nowadays, in Bihac and other areas, that all those proceedings are being tried based on the documentation collected by our bodies and our organs during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you're referring to. Are you referring to the proceedings and the trials that are being conducted now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I know that they're using documents that we had collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at what Simo Tusevljak had to say. He was the head of the Crime Department. Can we have the next page in both the English and Serbian, please. In English, that's page 20, in Serbian, 21. Here we see at the end of the second paragraph, where it says that criminal charges are pressed against everyone: "In Vlasenica alone, of 73 criminal charges, 23 were pressed against Serbs. For the time being, our most pressing task is to press criminal charges. War crimes are documented, even if they are committed by Serbs." Do you recall that this was the position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely correct. And it wasn't only his position. He did work in the Crime Department, but that was also the position of the minister as well as of all the other leaders, and this was shared also by chiefs of centres and stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it your impression at this meeting that there was a determined position that the police should do their work in a professional way, in a determined way, and irrespective of who the perpetrators were, irrespective of their ethnicity or faith?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we hear his answer? What did you say, Mr. Kezunovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that's absolutely true, that's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, can we see B/C/S version, page 17, and English, 16. It's the last paragraph on English. I think it's somewhere in the middle on page 16. It says: "At the end of this part of the meeting, there was a separate meeting among several people, among whom I included you." Did you find that paragraph? In English, we move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to this, you spoke about - can we go on - spoke about connections and the Criminal Code. I'm not sure whether it's a misinterpretation, but did you talk about Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a mistranslation. "KZ" means "Encryption" or "Cryptographic Protection," "Kripto Zastita."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 05297, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2765, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report by the MUP from the Romanija-Bircani CSB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they're responding to a document, strictly confidential, dated the 19th of July, 1992, number 1492, and they say: "In connection with the above-mentioned documents, which we received on 24 July, we are unable to provide data and reports in more detail due to the short time-limit for their delivery. "The most frequent problem in the preparation of data is weak communications with public security stations as a result of war operation." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then in the second paragraph, in the middle, it states: "Groups of persons in uniforms under arms are involved in the looting which creates the impression that it is a case of organised crime. Reports have it that most of these people are neither in the ranks of the army, nor the police. The crime-fighting section as well as the police are not able to take significant measurements and activities to prevent this. There are problems because we lacked sufficient number of cadres, as well as the fact that the military and the police are engaged on the front-lines." Is that correct, that anybody could wear a uniform, get weapons, and become some sort of force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this Security Centre, where there was no interruption in the territorial continuity, Birac, Romanija, Sarajevo, this person who wrote this said that he wasn't able to have good communication, even though everything was quite close; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But at the time when he was writing this, his location was in Lukavac, in the Energoinvest factory, and he had a large problem. He could see Ilidza, but he couldn't get to it. He needed half a day to go 'round to reach Ilidza. And I don't even want to talk about Ilijas, the other municipalities. His major problem was the fact that the city of Sarajevo, with the 10 pre-war municipalities, a large number of population, and - how shall I put it? - the line of separation was quite clumsy, and then there was the background, and then we were talking about whether Bratunac belongs to Sarajevo or not. And the name actually speaks for itself, Sarajevo-Romanija-Birac. That centre covered that area of Birac. And from Lukavica, it was hard for him to command and to keep it under control and to move around. That was a major problem to him; not only to him, but all the members of the service.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly have 65 ter 05631.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2767, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a periodical report, dated the 1st of July, covering the period up to the 30th of September; July, August and September for the Banja Luka, or the CSB area of Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the ERN, because there are certification pages in the document. I'm not sure which number it is. The ERN is 0074-9631. The document has been admitted. I just want to see what they say about communications at the end of this period in late September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this first paragraph, which states -- this is item 5, 5.1. Can we have the same in the English, please, 5.1, "Other Tasks and Assignments." And it states that in communications and cryptographic protection, repairs were made, objects' malfunctioning was repaired, and that during this period, non-coded dispatches and 152 coded dispatches were received. Is this much less than was actually needed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If you recall, some of the previous reports on the work that you showed yesterday, they encompass the period from the beginning of 1992, and actually a much larger of dispatches involved. So this is an incomparably lower number in comparison to the first quarter of that same 1992, before the conflict broke out. So this can indicate what the ratio was. It's some 10 or 15 times, as far as I can remember these figures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 0074-9641, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree -- let's look at this second paragraph in the middle. They're talking about the lack of materiel and technical equipment, out-dated equipment, worn-out equipment, shortage of spare parts, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is all correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have D473.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a summary from a working group meeting of the MUP management, held on the 20th of August, 1992, in Trebinje. Do you recall that this meeting was held in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at English page 3 and Serbian page 3 in the document. Actually, the page bears the number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It states at the top that the meeting was chaired by the minister. In the third paragraph, it says that there was an analysis of the implementation of the conclusions from the previous meeting. The fourth paragraph talks about removing from the MUP all those who are not at the requisite professional and moral level, and it also states that the army was dealing with combat activities, and the MUP can then carry out its function to fight crime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the following page both in the English and the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can I just add something else, which is quite a feature? And these days, this is a discussion ongoing regarding the change of laws in veterans' benefits, and the pension and retirement law and so on. All the policemen who went to the lines as fighters, when they returned, they didn't have any breaks or rests, but went back to their regular jobs, so that these people really were overloaded, not loaded, burdened, but over-burdened, and that was a characteristic feature in that period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 4 in the English and I think it's also page 4 in the Serbian. Yes, it's the following page in the Serbian too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Krsto Savic is speaking, and in the second paragraph it states: "Paramilitary groups are present in the area of the CSB but, following the minister's order, this problem was successfully resolved in co-operation with the Army of the Serbian Republic." So now there are remnants of those groups in some areas, like Nevesinje, where such formation used to number up to 200 members. Do you recall that there were arrests, pursuant to my general order and pursuant to the order of the minister, on the ban of military formations, and here we have, at this time in late August, this gentleman, Mr. Savic, reporting that this has already been cleared up, to a large degree, and do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and I do agree. Police even -- and this is somewhere in the documentation, I think, with the Prosecutor. There are lists of members of the police who were leaving the ranks of the police without returning their uniforms and official IDs, so it had to be established where they were, what they were doing, and the rest of that, specifically to prevent such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to save time by focusing as much as possible on your area of expertise. Thank you. Can we now have 1D3602. 1D3602.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this telegram of the 22nd of October, 1992. It's written by the under-secretary for the National Security Service. It's dispatched to all the sector of the National Security Service, and it states: "Since the communications system between the SNB and the seat and all SNB sectors is operative, in the future it is necessary that you inform us regularly ..." And so on and so forth. Do you agree that only on the 22nd of October, he could request that regular reports be sent in future, which implicitly means that up until that time, he could not state such requests because the communications were not satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I believe that this is absolutely correct, because it was in their interest to be able to communicate with everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you agree that he could ask this only on the 22nd of October?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, because you can see the date when this telegram or dispatch was sent.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1368, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3603, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that on the 15th of December, 1992, this is sent to all the CSBs and the SJBs, and the under-secretary of the SNB? It's a request by the minister for a report on the work, and then he goes on to state: "Measures and activities aimed at creating and the functioning of the MUP of Republika Srpska, information about the data on personnel ..." Can we have the following page, please. We can look at item B towards the end, the bullet point before last: To inform him about the number of MUP removed from the MUP they do not meet the criteria for work in the MUP, because of crimes committed before the 4th of April, 1992; 2, for crimes committed after April 4th, 1992; and for other reasons making them unfit to work in the MUP organs; and four, because of criminal charges submitted against workers of the MUP of Republica Srpska, property crimes, and so on and so forth. Do you recall that here, at the end of year 1992, he is asking to be regularly informed about how ranks of the police are being cleansed of unsuitable members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the -- if they are talking about the number of criminal charges submitted, can we have the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It goes on to Article G. We need to look at the following page in the English, total number of crimes, total number of criminal charges. And then they are talking about the number of criminal reports that were recorded. Do you agree that the ministry at the seat was very strict and demanded complete adherence to the Rules of Service and to the law?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct. While you were reading these certain points, I just glanced at the rest of the things written, and everything is stated here in the same way it would be during peacetime, plus it takes into account wartime activities of the minister. Before he became a minister, worked in the Crime Investigation Section of the police, so he's a professional and knows his job.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page, where we can look at Roman II.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Roman II --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the reference, please, in the text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we would like to have the reference in the text. The reading is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you were too fast and the interpreters couldn't follow. If you could repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the third paragraph, where it states here: "In order for the MUP report to be ready in time to be presented to the Government, Assembly and Presidency of the Republika Srpska, the centre shall submit reports by the 5th of January, 1993, at the latest. The chiefs of centres and administrations shall be held personally responsible for the timeliness and accuracy of data and assessments."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Presidency, the Government and the Assembly were periodically informed about the work of the MUP, as well as briefly about the data according to the questionnaire sent by the minister?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I think that that was, indeed, the case, because these reports had been done before the war to inform the government and other agencies that needed to have them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1369, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I would like to tell you that your time is almost up. You have about 10 minutes, or 15, so try to finish it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to do that. But before that, I'd like to show 65 ter 04250 and ask the witness to mark this map; in fact, to mark the deployment of infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this map, Witness, and then I will show you another one so that you can tell us which one would make it easier for you to mark, to show the main nodes or centres, and what you had to reconnect? Now, could we have D484? But in the meantime, are you familiar with this map? This map shows the ethnic distribution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is familiar. I don't know what period this relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It relates to 1991. It's from the census of 1991. But are you aware that the fighting actually followed these ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D484, please. And could the witness be assisted with the electronic pen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, would it be easier for you to mark this map to show the centres, the main nodes, the communication nodes, and the main relay stations on it? Could the Usher please assist the witness with the electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will give you a brief reply. All the networks, both telephone and teleprinter networks, had the node. The main node was in Sarajevo, at the Telecommunications Centre building. Such telecommunications centres existed in all regional centres, in other words in Banja Luka, Bihac, Prijedor, Livno, Mostar, Tuzla, Gorazde; in other words, in 10 centres. If, in Banja Luka alone, and Doboj, and of course Prijedor too, but at this time point in time Prijedor was just a public security station, now all of those facilities were controlled by Serbs, but in all other areas and, crucially, in Sarajevo, which was the main node from which all the communications spread out to all other centres in the republic, and also towards other republics and federal institutions, all of those were controlled by the other side. So simply put, by simply plugging out these systems in Sarajevo, they could disable all of these centres. So it's really completely irrelevant what -- where these -- all of these lines -- or how they ran, along which routes, because that's really just a secondary issue, because they were able, both in peacetime and also in wartime, to disable all those communication by plugging them out from Sarajevo. So they kept their own communications live, whereas they plugged or cut off the communications controlled by Serbs. Now, I don't know if you need me to mark this. I could, but this is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to -- I would like you to mark it. But would it be easier to use the other map, the ethnic map, as it were? Could you just show us the routes that the communications ran? Could you please put little squares to indicate the main nodes, and mark the ones that were under the control of the Muslims in red, and in blue for the ones controlled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here we have Sarajevo, Mostar. They had them [marks]. Bihac, let me find it. Bihac [marks]. Tuzla [marks], Gorazde [marks], Livno [marks], Zenica [marks]. All of these centres were -- remained in their -- under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you please use the blue pen to mark what remained under our control?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here it is. It's Banja Luka [marks], Prijedor [marks], and Doboj. Let me see where that was. Yeah, here it is [marks]. However, all the rest that was part of the Serbian territory was connected or linked up to the centres that were under their control. Now, I don't know what colour pen I should use to show that. But, for instance, Trebinje, the entire area of Stari Herzegovina all the way to Trebinje, was linked up to Gorazde and Mostar. Brcko, Bijeljina, Zvornik, Bratunac, all of that was linked or gravitated towards Tuzla; in other words, the entire area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate these areas by marking them with arrows?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, here, Trebinje [marks]. I didn't quite get it, but it doesn't really matter. All of these municipalities here were linked up to Mostar. The ones here, they gravitated towards Gorazde, they links in Gorazde [marks], these municipalities around here, Rudo, Visegrad. Now, Rogatica was linked with Sarajevo [marks]. All areas around Brcko, Bijeljina, Zvornik, they were connected or linked up with Tuzla, including Srebrenica, Vlasenica and so on [marks]. Well, I don't even have to mark Bihac because that was, anyhow, territory under the control of that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the Serb municipalities of Petrovac, Drvar, Kljuc? Where did they have their links?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in part, they had links in Banja Luka and in other -- and part of them had links in Bihac. I am not absolutely certain, but in any case, they were linked up to areas, to centres that were under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Glamoc and Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were connected and linked up to Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please date and sign this map?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1370, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last document. I would appreciate the understanding of the Prosecution. This is a document that was not on the list, but it's 65 ter 18342. And perhaps we can mark it for identification, because we don't have a translation, but we would like to use this document as it arose from something the witness said, and we would like to take advantage of this witness being here. So, that's 65 ter 18342, could we have it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is a meeting of an expanded session -- or, rather, minutes from an expanded meeting of the Professional Collegium of the Ministry of the Interior, and we see here that your name is mentioned in the third line from the bottom, where a list is given of the participants?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have a translation, I'll have to read this slowly. We can see here that part of the session was attended by the counsel to the minister, Kusmuk, the commander, Karisik and so on. Now, could we have the third page, please. By the way, did you know these people, Kusmuk and Milenko Karisik?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Milenko Karisik the deputy commander of the joint Special Brigade, the commander of which was Dragan Vikic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, was Karisik, Milenko, a very strict man when it came to conditions for those who wanted to join his unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now take a look at the third paragraph from the top, where Trebinje is mentioned and it says: "We have to resolve all our weaknesses ... "." And it says: "It was emphasised one more time that only those individuals who met the legal requisites to work in the organs of the interior can become members of the service, and we have to rid our ranks of those individuals who committed acts, that they should not be -- deliberately committed acts which were not legitimate." Now, there is an error in the transcript. There is Dragan Vikic, that's the name, and do you agree that he was the commander of the joint brigade, he was a Muslim, and Milenko Karisik was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and I believe this was called the Special Detachment of the Republic SUP, and the commander was Vikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see from this paragraph that Milenko Karisik did not allow criminals to join his unit, and that he stressed that in this meeting, which you attended as well, and it was re-affirmed that this was the position, that the police should always be rid of such individuals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we can see it from this text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 6. I'm not exactly sure. That's AD-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, it says: "The minister also ordered that, like what was done in the SJB in Zvornik, rigorous action be taken against chiefs of SJBs, including dismissals, if so necessary, because of their failure to report to CSB and MUP." Does this show that the minister was completely reliant on the information that he received and that there were some errors in the reporting system; in other words, that the minister was misinformed at some times?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances as well, and it is also true that he was completely dependent on what was being reported to him from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it would appear that those people did not really report their own errors; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably so, as we see that he was upset about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then under "AD-2," Minister Stanisic describes why it was necessary to establish a Special Brigade of the police, bearing in mind that the state is being established, and that in wartime conditions, there is an emergence of destructive forces which are attempting to subvert it, and so on and so forth. And he explains that this is why the Special Brigade had to be established. Now, do you remember whether this Special Brigade arrested members of paramilitary units in Zvornik, but also elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It would appear, based on that, that Minister Stanisic had established the Special Brigade because it was necessary to support law and order on the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we see that there's a proposal to review all the registrations of vehicles because there were cases of vehicle thefts, and then there is also mention that there is general chaos in this respect. And then in the third paragraph, it says that: "The chiefs of CSB are also duty-bound to make a complete list of the entire property of the MUP and to do a review from the beginning of the war of all the items that had been seized, especially money and valuables. And then it says: "At the proposal of the chief of the Administration for Communications and Encryption, we support the organising of a course for training personnel for encryption." Were you the chief of that administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why were such courses necessary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely because we didn't have enough men who could encode messages, written messages as well as all others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And we're talking about the 5th of November, 1992, right, in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's time for you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have one or two questions related to this document, and then I will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, under paragraph 4, in the second paragraph we see that there were questions from certain SJBs whether it was allowed to -- whether citizens were allowed to change their first and last name, citizens of non-Serb nationality, and it was concluded that in such cases, one should act according to the law, and that the SJB should have special record-keeping in such instances. So there were instances where people wanted to change their names, correct, and it was required that that should be done according to the law; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we don't -- I don't have any other questions. I would like to tend this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps we can just put an MFI, pending its translation, unless Mr. Gaynor has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just a couple of observations. No objection to its MFI'd. This document wasn't on the list, nor was D447, and I think we had about 12 or 13 pages of cross-examination about D447. So we would request notification, even if it's by late evening, of additions like this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. We'll mark this document for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1371, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kezunovic, thank you very much, and may I just say that I am sorry that we haven't met before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, and good luck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, could I call up P2765.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, earlier today you were asked a few questions about this document which you'll see on the screen in front of you, and the question was put to you as follows: "This person who wrote this said that he wasn't able to have good communication, even though everything was quite close; isn't that correct?" And your answer, you said that: "Yes, that is correct." And then you went to point out that his location was at Lukavac, and he could see Ilidza, but he couldn't get to it. "He needed half a day to go 'round to reach Ilidza, and I don't even want to talk about Ilijas, the other municipalities." Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we look at the bottom of page 2 in English, going on to the top of page 3 in English. And if we could look at the bottom of page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you see a reference there to communications between this CSB and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which line is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's halfway down the page in your version. It's the third-last paragraph, the fourth-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So you accept that this CSB was in contact with the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not mean that this was -- how do you mean; in contact, physically, that somebody would go to the command, or are you thinking of links, communications?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Communications links. There were communications links?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't have that, they didn't have communication. What it says here, that they handed over such and such a number of written documents. It was either delivered by courier or some other way. You can see that it says that some information was also given orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct. If we could go to the next page in English. We can stay on the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, at the top of this, we see a reference to: "100 written and a significant number of oral reports to the units in the field (Vogosca, Ilijas, Ilidza, Hadzici, Pale, Sokolac and Han Pijesak)." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you, therefore, accept, yes or no, that there was, in fact, communication from this CSB to Ilijas and Ilidza, as well as the other areas mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, just briefly, that communication did exist, but it's a question of at which point it was working and at which point it wasn't, for the different reasons that I cited during the testimony; power cuts, something that broke down, things like that. If everything was working, in principle, within the municipality, there was communication, but that does not mean that this was available continuously at all times. Especially in this area, a lot of power cuts occurred, and that would be enough to knock the communications out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another point, and that is -- at pages 18 and 19 today, you were shown a document signed by the minister on the 22nd of October, 1992, and a question was put to you: "Do you agree that only on the 22nd of October, he could request that regular reports be sent in future, which implicitly means that up until that time he could not state such requests because communications were not satisfactory?" And you said that you agreed, and you believed that to be absolutely correct. Do you remember that exchange?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you described for us - this was at pages 14950 to 14951 - the process by which the daily bulletins were issued by the minister, and you said that: "The bulletins which during the previous 24 hours covered the events would be sent by the Public Security Station officials and combined into one report which would be sent to their superior security centre, which put it all together into one report and sent it to the ministry at the headquarters." Do you recall your evidence about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, although this translation is a little bit confusing. But I understand the sense; I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Essentially, you're telling us that the SJBs would communicate reports to the CSBs, and the CSBs would collate the information within their area of operation and provide that to the ministry? Is that a reasonable summary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained that for these problems, the Analysis and Information Administration was in charge of. This is not my area. As for communications links, I recognise elements in the dispatch, and I confirm that and I draw possible conclusions. I explained that several times already. I don't know what was instructed in the minister's dispatch, whether the Public Security Stations should directly report back or should they sent a report to the centre, and then the centre would put them all of them together and send them to the MUP. I don't know that. I don't know, I don't remember what the original source dispatch from the minister said. If there was an order for each station to send back a report, then that's probably how it was done. If it was ordered by the stations to send their reports to the centres, for the centres then to make a collective report and send it to the ministry, that's probably how it was done. It was done as ordered. So now I really don't remember what the original dispatch by the minister said, even though you showed it, but I didn't really pay attention. As far as I'm concerned, this is of lesser importance. The important thing is for the information to reach their destination. Of lesser importance is the type of organisation, you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, I'd prefer to carry on, if I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just what is it? You were going to object to something, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an objection, because we're talking about state security here, but Mr. Gaynor continues to ask about public security. These are two separate services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not helpful. Please carry on, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, yesterday you were shown a series of daily reports issued by the minister, starting, I think, with Report 3 and going up to Report 109, 111, 113. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember, but the reports were not drafted by the minister, but by the Administration for Analysis and Information Affairs, and they acted pursuant to the instructions by the minister. They didn't send anything back to the minister because there are two situations. One is a collation of everything that happened during a certain period, and then this is sent in order to make a kind of report. The second thing is sending a report on any kind of event of interest, from the intelligence point of view, and that is something that is reported upon immediately in order for action to be, perhaps, taken. You understand, if something happened, anything which was of interest in the security sense, then perhaps it's necessary for some unit to intervene in the field, and a report about that is sent immediately. That later, then, is included in the general overview in the bulletin. The bulletin is just a collective review of all the events that happened over a certain period of time. It's not an operative document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the bulletins which you were shown yesterday, dated mainly from April and May of 1992, and as we saw yesterday, they covered events taking place in municipalities falling within the area of responsibility of Banja Luka CSB as well as Bijeljina CSB and other CSBs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So at least during the early months after the establishment of the RS MUP, there was capacity for those reports to be drafted at the seat of the MUP, in accordance with the procedure you've described; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection. Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you reformulate?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll reformulate, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: During that period, April and May of 1992, Mr. Kezunovic, was there, yes or no, capacity for the CSBs in Banja Luka and Bijeljina and elsewhere to provide information to the seat of the ministry for insertion into the daily report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm repeating the same thing. I cannot answer with a yes or no, because, in principle, they can, but there were countless problems for each specific day, so I don't know whether they were able to deliver that for each specific day, because you could see in a lot of the documents, only two centres provide reports and some information and three of them do not for that particular day. I don't know if they provided the documents the following day, the third day, the fourth day, whenever they were able to. That is something that I don't know. I wasn't really monitoring them. All I can do is to interpret what is written in the document. You could see that two delivered and three did not, and that is something that I can say for each document. But the general conclusion as to whether it could have been, perhaps it could have been, but perhaps it could have not. I repeat, there were countless problems, combat actions, power cuts, failures, and sometimes it was true that communications were not working continuously along all directions. Sometimes there were interruptions, so it's difficult to give a general assessment. It's much easier to give an answer for each specific case, even with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Finally, I'd like to clarify one small point. Yesterday, at page 14995, a couple of questions were put to you about the log-book of Prijedor SJB, which was the first exhibit you were shown during your direct, and the question that was put to you was: "Would you agree that everything that was received by Prijedor was from its immediate vicinity, Banja Luka, Bosanski Novi, and so on?" And then you went on to give your answer about that. I want you to clarify for Their Honours that after the establishment of the RS MUP, was Prijedor a CSB or was it an SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an SJB, a public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And was it the practice, generally speaking, for an SJB in the Krajina to communicate directly with entities over in Eastern Bosnia? Was that the general method by which SJBs would give their information to the minister?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know now. I don't understand the question. What does it mean, "over in Eastern Bosnia," and then you mention the minister? In which context?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll reformulate my point. You've explained already the process by which SJBs would provide reports to CSBs, and CSBs would then provide a collated report to the minister. My question is this: Would you ordinarily expect an SJB located within the area of responsibility of Banja Luka CSB, such as Prijedor SJB, would you ordinarily expect that level of police station to be in direct contact with, for example, SJBs in Eastern Bosnia or with the seat of the ministry in Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why they would do that. That's why there was an organisation of the ministry in the way that it existed, so that everything was resolved in the way that if something happened in the field, first of all, it happened in the territory of some public security station area, regardless of whether there was a CSB in that town. The SJB was in charge, primarily, of maintaining law and order, dealing with crimes and things like that that are under the jurisdiction of the MUP. The SJB is in charge of things like that first. Since a problem could have something to do affecting the neighbouring municipalities, the organisation is set up in such a way that the CSB is in charge of co-ordinating things like that. It co-ordinates within a region. If co-operation between two SJBs is required, which are, for example, in different regions, for example, one, let's say belongs to Bijeljina and the other one belongs to Doboj, but they are boundary, neighbouring stations, but from two different regions, then the matter has to be also carried through to the authorised CSBs. Because they are better equipped, they have better trained personnel, police crime investigation inspectors and other experts. And in that way the manner of communication is set up in such a way that the stations exclusively communicate to the centres, and the centres communicate with the ministry, because the ministry is at the top of that overall problem matter along the lines of work. It doesn't make sense for the Trebinje SJB to be sending something to the Gradiska SJB unless they are, for example, providing the name of the owner of a vehicle who comes from Trebinje and has created a problem in Gradiska. Only things like that were resolved directly among the municipalities. Otherwise, it all went up to the CSBs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kezunovic. No further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kezunovic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal, I thank you for your coming to the Tribunal to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together. It's time to have a break. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sorry to disturb you. I wanted to advise you of some developments that had taken place with respect to Mr. Ristic. And we have filed, a few minutes ago, the 52nd motion for finding of disclosure violation and a motion to exclude his testimony entirely. The most recent developments is that today, the Prosecution has informed us that they neglected to disclose to us two statements of this very witness, Mr. Nebojsa Ristic, which were taken by the Ministry of Interior of the Republika Srpska and which we suspected, from the interview, may have been in the possession of the Office of the Prosecution. This is another violation of Rule 66(A)(2), and one which the Prosecution has conceded in their response to our 51st motion. So this will affect our preparation, obviously. But more so than that, we think that this is -- the time has come where the Chamber has to do something more than put a Band-Aid on a small cut, because these disclosure violations are pouring in at an unprecedented rate, well after your final dead-line for disclosure, and we simply can't continue to operate this way. I know if that if we hustle and scratch around, we can find a few extra hours to accommodate these violations, but it's completely unfair for a trial to be conducted in this manner, where the burden is on us to interrupt our preparation, to scramble around, when the Prosecution is responsible entirely for unjustified and inexcusable violations of the rules of disclosure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it, Mr. Tieger, that you are minded to file your response in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, these interviews are dealt with in the response we just filed. What Mr. Robinson is aware of, and fails to mention, or at least I believe he's aware of it, is that these interviews are irrelevant to the events during the indictment period and are of a very -- relatively short nature. In any event, it's dealt in the motion, the need for oral submissions to supplement the written filing is difficult to see, as is the stridency of the language used in the submission, so the Court will see what this matter is about in the filing that was made earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you'll not respond to this separately? All we have to do is to read your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm happy to look at it again to see if any further information for the Court is necessary. But as I say, we dealt with it in the filing. I think that will be sufficient. If further information appears necessary, we'll let the Court know right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if there's anything for you to raise, then do it by the close of business today. Thank you. Before we bring in the witness, shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Take your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor from the Prosecution will ask you some questions. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ranko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've previously testified for this Tribunal in the trial of Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've previously met with members of the Office of the Prosecutor and provided information to them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've reviewed an amalgamated statement containing relevant portions of your testimony from the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, as well as other information that you've provided to the Prosecution; is that true?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's true. However, I would like to take this opportunity to say that all the statements were shown to me in the English language, and I only speak Serbian, and this although I requested that I be provided these statements in my mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was the amalgamated statement read back to you in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were read back to me, but there were some issues in one part of the statement with the word "ostali," because that word can have -- its meaning is twofold in our language. It can mean -- it can relate to a person and others or it can be a verb where it would mean "we remained" in a certain area. The same word would be used in Serbian. Subsequently, when I checked the text, I realised that that word remained in the text of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to consult with someone who speaks both English and B/C/S as to the form of the translation used in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: When I was interviewed at the Office of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in Sarajevo, in Nedzarici, I requested that the interpreter provided be from my own nation, that that person speak Serbian. However, because of some personal reason, that personal could not attend, so that I had an interpreter who was of Bosniak ethnicity. They said that that word in part of my statement was, in fact, quite appropriate, as far as the structure of the sentence was concerned. However, I requested that it be checked because this word, "ostali," which can mean either "the others" or "to remain," that it should be -- that it should actually remain, because if it was skipped and taken out, that then it would completely alter the sense of the sentence, and this in context of an order which was issued on the 29th of April, 1992, by the commander of the then BH Army -- or, rather, the BH TO, Territorial Defence, Mr. Hasan Efendic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps the easiest way to clarify the position would be to bring up the document in question and ask the witness to clarify which word he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Which paragraph is he referring to? Let's bring up the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 22912. This particular exhibit is discussed by the witness on page 33 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you see the order of Hasan Efendic in front of you, do you?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed, could you -- you said page 33 of his amalgamated statement. Do you know which part he is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm somewhat unclear, but I believe the translation difficulty might arise out of the document, itself. It's not a translation difficulty in the statement. But I'm hoping to clarify that with the witness right now, that the word which was in discussion between the interpreter and the witness appears in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's first proceed with this document. I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, do you see in this document the reference that you're concerned about?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That word does not appear in the document, itself. However, during the interview and during the investigation, a question was put to me where I was asked to explain a sentence, where I replied -- in reply to the question, I said that we remained as part of the communications system of the former Territorial Defence and BH Army, so that they were able, in all the documents that they sent to their subordinate units in the period of the month of April and May, if those messages were sent to all units, then we would have received them at our centre at Pale. In other words, we remained within their system of communications, remained, "ostali".

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. The reference is, in fact, from the middle of the witness's statement, page 33, and perhaps I can read the words to you, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we bring it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, it's -- 90245 is the 65 ter number, and if we can go to page 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Vukovic, I will read the question to you and I will read the answer to you, and then you can make whatever clarifications necessary. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The question is as follows: "Let's just clarify one thing. That communications centre, that belonged to the city of Sarajevo, with which you were linked, as you say, that was under the control of the Muslim forces; right?" Your answer reads as follows: "When we were part of the line of command of the city centre, that was before the conflict started. In 1992, in the month of April, we remained linked with the same city centre, and we could still communicate with them freely." That's the end of the quote. Would you like to clarify your answer in any way?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the tendency of my explanation. On the critical day, when that order was sent from the teleprinter of the republic centre for communications and encryption and monitoring and information, from the Executive Council building, or, rather, from the Republican Secretariat of National Defence, as it was called at the time, from a teleprinter machine which was on the 14th floor, a TX-100, manufactured by EI Nis, we received that order because it was sent to a number of different addressees. And in that way, we received it as well, it found its way to our desks at our centre. At the time, the communications were still intact, the communications between all of those different users which had been part of the Republic Secretariat of National Defence. So the communications had still been intact, and in this way we received that order at Pale as well. And I believe this is sufficient, by way of explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. If we look at the first page of your amalgamated statement, please. Is that your signature on the first page?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As we've discussed previously, there is a typographical error. It says that you reviewed this statement on the 23rd and 24th of May, 2011, and we have to correct that, because you reviewed this statement on the 23rd, the 24th, and the 25th of May, 2011; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As I discussed with you previously, I want to note two minor typographical errors. Paragraph 77 refers to 65 ter 29798. The correct number is 65 ter 21798. Second, footnote 115 that's on the page we were looking at earlier refers to 65 ter 22910 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you say page 67?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, the first erratum refers to paragraph 77. The second refers to footnote 115. That refers to 65 ter 22910. The correct number is 22912.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Subject to the clarification that you provided to the Court, and to the three typographical corrections we've just made, do you adopt the amalgamated statement as your evidence? And if you were questioned today about the same issues, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I propose -- first of all, I would like to tender the statement, and I would propose to read a summary of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2794, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Ranko Vukovic was the chief of the Republic Communications Centre in Pale for the duration of the 1992-to-1995 conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the public, what you're doing is reading out the summary of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The primary purpose of the Republic Communications Centre was to provide oral and written communications links to civilian authorities in Pale, including the RS Presidency, Assembly and Government. The Republic Communications Centre was equipped with telephone lines, switchboards, teleprinters, fax, radio and radio-relay equipment. It also used couriers. Radovan Karadzic's office in Pale was connected to the Republic Communications Centre by a secure telephone line.
