Mr. Vukovic describes the methods used to keep the Republic Communications Centre in contact with the regional communications centres. The Republic Communications Centre was connected to the VRS Main Staff Communications Centre by radio relay and by the PTT network. The VRS Main Staff Communications Centre was located in a former JNA facility situated deep underground in Crna Rijeka, near Han Pijesak. The transmitters for the Crna Rijeka Communications Centre were located on Veliki Zep, a hill above Crna Rijeka. Communications from Pale to various parts of territory under Bosnian Serb control were routed through the VRS Main Staff Communications Centre at Crna Rijeka. Maintenance teams for the VRS 67th Communications Regiment at Han Pijesak would come to repair the Republic Communications Centre's equipment as necessary and very quickly. The system functioned well during the war. Mr. Vukovic identifies communications sent from Karadzic to the VRS Main Staff using the link from the Republic Communications Centre to the VRS Main Staff Communications Centre at Crna Rijeka. He also identifies documents sent from Crna Rijeka to other locations, such as the commands of the corps of the VRS. It was usually possible for the Republic Communications Centre to connect Karadzic to whomever he wished to contact. Karadzic's office also sometimes used the RS MUP communications network and had access to its own couriers. The RS MUP Communications Centre in Pale was separate from the Republic Communications Centre and used a separate communications system, but the Republic Communications Centre assisted the RS MUP organs with their communication if they were having difficulty with their own system. Mr. Vukovic provides his comments on a selection of documents, including communications between the Presidency and the VRS Main Staff, as well as communications log-books and documents sent by the RS MUP communications system in 1995 concerning security for convoys containing Karadzic. That ends the summary for the benefit of the public. I want to return briefly to two points arose in that summary, but they're listed in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe very briefly, Mr. Vukovic, the relationship between the RS MUP Communications Centre in Pale and your centre, the Republic Communications Centre?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Communications Centre of the MUP had its own independent system of communications. In other words, they did not depend on the Ministry of Defence, but, rather, they used the Republic Communications Centre at Pale. They developed their own documents, independent of us, and they also developed their plans of work of radio communications. They had trained staff to do that. But in the beginning, and I'm referring to the communication centres at Pale, the MUP Communications Centre, where Paunovic, Milenko -- the late Milenko Paunovic worked. They had trouble hiring staff which had military specialties from the Signals Corps, and we would assist them with that. We would assist them to identify the required personnel that was deficient, that they were short in. Now, at the Republic Communications Centre throughout the combat operations, throughout the war, we had also personnel problems, and in those conditions we managed to carry out all the tasks that were required of us, sometimes successfully, but sometimes not as successfully, and sometimes we broke through the dead-lines that were asked of us because we had difficulties in maintaining the communications lines, because frequently they would break down and be out of operation. And until they were re-established, we had to use other means of communications that we developed and kept on standby as a back-up system precisely because we had frequent problems with the lines going down, so that it was really with super-human efforts that we managed to maintain communications throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one minute, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I forgot to tell you that if you need a break at any time, don't hesitate to let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, in your statement you refer to the 67th Communications Regiment of the VRS. Insofar as you know, what do you understand the role or mandate of the 67th Communications Regiment was?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. From the aspect of the functioning of the Republican Communications Centre, I cannot assess the operation of the communications unit of the Main Staff, the 67th Communications Regiment, because I'm not competent to evaluate their positions and their manner and method of work, and I cannot talk about that either, because I stated -- I gave the solemn declaration, I'm holding to it, and it obliges me to speak about only those things that I can talk about competently. As for the 67th Communications Regiment, I can say that we often repaired our equipment through them, equipment that we had in our centre, and that we always were met with understanding, professionalism, good attitude, because they had personnel that was trained to maintain certain communications equipment that we were unable to fix in our own workshops. The 67th Communications Regiment, by establishment, was duty-bound to assist either us, or the MUP, or anyone in the case this was required, if we had problems with communications, with means and equipment, with training, for certain deficient specialties in the VS. They -- for example, when we were equipping centres with new equipment, in case we needed some experts which could only be trained by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, this was done because we didn't have any way of training one or two of these people, because what was required was to create some kind of model environment to work. And there was a special unit in the 67th Communications Regiment that provided training, but I can say that in all aspects of service that had to do with communications, their attitude was very professional. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your answer, you referred to the abbreviation "VS." Could you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not "VS," it's "VES." This is the military occupation specialty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I request 65 ter 23143, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in a moment, Mr. Vukovic, on the screen in front of you, you'll see a map, and it's one you've seen before. If you could, first of all, just tell Their Honours what you understand the map to be. I beg your pardon. This is a diagram. We're coming to the map. If you can explain to Their Honours what you understand, in general terms, this diagram to be, and then I will ask you some specific questions about it.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot interpret the diagram of the protected communications of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. But as for the part relating to communications between the Main Staff of the VRS and the Communications Centre -- the Republican Communications Centre in Pale, I can speak about those particular branches and the connection with the stationary communications centre at Pale and the stationary communications centre at Crna Rijeka. This is a little bit unclear. I cannot really see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Kezunovic. Could I ask the Registrar to expand the central box, the one big box that we see at the centre. Now, in the top right-hand corner of the screen in front of you, Mr. Vukovic, you see "SCV Veliki Zep." Could you tell us what that means, please?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This is not "SCV Veliki Zep," but this is the stationary node "SCV."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And could you just expand the abbreviation for us? "SCV" refers to what?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Stationary Communications Node, Veliki Zep, is located at the command post of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and this diagram should be interpreted by the senior officer who made it from the Army of Republika Srpska. I can recognise some communications here which began or ended at the stationary communications hub at Veliki Zep or the one in Pale. This is an automatic telephone exchange which ended in the offices of the president of the Republika Srpska and the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. These were automatic telephone exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I interrupt for a minute there. In the box in the top right-hand corner of the screen in front of us, we see, as the seventh and eighth entries, "ATC G-1 Predsed.RS." The next one refers to "Pr.Skup.RS." Are those the two entries you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at that box, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, the box in the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Top right-hand corner in this box?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, the box on the screen in front of us in the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what you understand "Predsed.RS" and "Pr.skup.RS" mean yes?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The first one is Pr, "Predsednik," that is, president of the RS, meaning that this extension was in the office of the president of Republika Srpska. This extension, 171, "Prsk" means the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska. That extension was in the Cabinet of the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, according to this particular scheme.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to clarify the point: After the Presidency, we see the number 230, and after the president of the Assembly, we see the number 171. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, a few entries further down, we see "Preds.VL.RS," followed by the number 182. Could you tell us what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. This the prime minister's office of Republika Srpska, and this was extension 182.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could zoom out, please, and look at the top right-hand corner under, first of all, the box marked "SCV Jahorina," which is under the box marked. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Again, I think we can see, under number 7 here, a reference to the Presidency of the RS, and, number 8, a reference to the president of the Assembly of the RS. Could you confirm that, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this. This is a stationary communications node at the Jahorina facility, from the radio-relay communications diagram of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska. Again, I note, I cannot discuss or talk about that, because this is not really my jurisdiction. I'm not competent to interpret the diagram of radio communications of the army. But 7 and 8, those items refer to the radio-relay connections between the Cabinet of the president of Republika Srpska and the Cabinet of the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, with the stationary hub at Veliki Zep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could we zoom out a bit again, Mr. Registrar, please, and zoom in on the box marked "Pale."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The last two entries in this box, again, Mr. Vukovic, could you clarify what they are?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: These two last entries show that these numbers, 230 and 171, ended at the offices in Pale of the president of Republika Srpska and the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska via an automatic telephone exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not going to translate this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The existing translation does not contain the translations of everything inside it, but we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have an English translation. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, the English translation that's been up-loaded simply gives the title of the graph, but does not indicate the entities within the graph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that the translation would help us. We'll admit it as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I please ask for 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But just for the purpose, could you read the title on the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you read that title, please, Mr. Vukovic? Perhaps we can zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The heading of the document is "Diagram of the --" wait, I've lost it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have that translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registrar, please, for 65 ter 04325. In a moment, you'll be seeing the map I promised earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you could explain to Their Honours, briefly, before I ask you any questions about it, what you believe the map to be? It will be on your screen in a moment. Sorry, the 65 ter number of the map should be 04325. Perhaps we could zoom in a little on the top portion of the map to assist Mr. Vukovic. Could you tell us what this map appears to be?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The map shows the communication connections plan of the Drina Corps in defence, approved by Major General Radislav Krstic, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see, in the middle of the map, the Cyrillic letters "IBK"?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't, no. No, no, I see it, I see it. Large letters standing for "Eastern Bosnia Corps," "IBK."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we move down the map a little bit, please. Now, if we could centre in on the centre of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: First of all, on the right, you see large Cyrillic letters "DK"?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I do, "Drina Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And on the left-hand of the map a little further down, you see "SRK" in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we zoom in, please, on the flag with the five Cyrillic letters under it. If we could zoom in a little more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this represents?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This represents the command post of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the radio-relay hub Veliki Zep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The five Cyrillic letters mean what?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: "The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska," "GS VRS."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Underneath that, we see a box. Inside the box are the letters "V. Zep." What is that?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That is a hill where the Stationary Communications Centre of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was located. That is the radio-relay hub.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we could -- first of all, you see on your left another box at Han Pijesak. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What do you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This shows the Han Pijesak PTT. This is the forward command post at Han Pijesak, the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could I ask the Registrar to follow the line down from Han Pijesak. You can see a straight line. If we could just follow that line down the map, please. And a bit further down, please. And could you go a little bit further south, please, Mr. Registrar. Sorry, a little further west. We need to get over to the left-hand side of the -- very good, and carry on, and a little further south. Now, could we zoom in there a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see the town of Pale on this map?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see the non-straight line, the line which looks like it's following a road from Pale, which meets the straight line that we've just followed down from Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you understand that to be?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I note that I'm not competent or authorised to interpret the scheme of radio-relay connections of the Drina Corps in any shape or form, nor am I competent to interpret any kind of connections leading from the Main Staff to subordinate units. I can help here to say that this is the diagram showing how radio communications of the Army of Republika Srpska functioned, but it does not show that the Republican Communications Centre was part of it, the one that was located in Pale. However, however, since these radio-relay routes going from the Main Staff, from Veliki Zep, to all the subordinate units, then the radio-relay node that we looked at just now in Jahorina is, of course, part of the radio-relay connections shown on the diagram, and the Republican Communications Centre had a priority in providing certain services to the institutions of the civilian government. Then it had the priority of being allowed access to the communications system of the army, which means that we were obliged to help one another, and we were at each other's disposal, which was something that was expected of us. This diagram talks about the connections of the Army of Republika Srpska, showing the connections of the Main Staff and the subordinate corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does -- this particular map that we've just been inspecting, does it show the entirety of the radio-relay network of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This part of the radio-relay connection on this map does not show the complete radio-relay communications of the Army of Republika Srpska. This is only a part of it, covering the Drina Corps, the Main Staff and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So based on what I see here, I don't see the diagram in order to be able to say that this represents the entire network of the Army of Republika Srpska. This is only one section of it, showing the communications of the Main Staff, the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. That's what I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I tender that map, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2796, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up, please, 65 ter 23144.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you, first of all, read out the title at the top of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, this is a diagram of radio relay and wire links of the Drina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if you could help us with a few things. You see the large box to the right which is marked "Veliki Zep." Could we home in on that, please.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this represents, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This square represents the stationary communications hub at Veliki Zep. It was located at Veliki Zep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We see coming out of this straight lines, and we also see a curled line which goes to Crna Rijeka. Could you clarify this difference between straight lines and curled lines, as a general matter, on communications maps?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have radio-relay communications here, which are shown with a straight line, full straight line, and this curly line is a wire communications line, communications established through wire communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On this map, if we could zoom out of the map, please, we see a number of circles with flags on them. Could you tell us what a circle with a flag on it denotes?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The circle marks the place where a certain communications unit, or a communications centre is located, or where a certain command of a unit is located, or a socio-political organ, or a social political community, civilian organs. On the diagram, I can see that this covers the distribution of the radio-relay and wire communications in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, this particular map doesn't happen to show any connection to the town of Pale. Would you be able to explain why that is?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't show Pale because this is a unit subordinated to the Main Staff of the VRS and not to the civilian authorities that were based in Pale. So this is a diagram of communications between units of the VRS. And, again, I have to say that I'm neither competent nor authorised to discuss this, because this was prepared -- this diagram was prepared by an officer of the Drina Corps Command, a communications officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2797, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I now call up, please, 65 ter 02655.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There's a map coming up now, Mr. Vukovic, which was provided to us by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm not going to ask you about what it purports to depict. We're just going to look at one small part of the map. Could we -- could you tell us what the title of the map appears to be, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a working map of the Section for Counter-Electronic Combat of the 2nd Corps, Counter-Electronic Surveillance of the 2nd Krajina Corps, but I can't really see clearly. What I can see is that this is a map for counter-electronic surveillance of the 2nd Corps of the BH Army, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registrar just to go down to the very bottom of the map. In fact, that will do for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see the straight lines that we see on this map?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you be able to comment in any way as to what they might represent?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They might represent radio-relay routes of the commands that developed certain communications centres in these areas. I'm not really the best-placed person to interpret this. I don't know what units or what armed forces developed these communications centres. This is something that probably relates to the BH Army, the so-called BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness may be assisted by seeing the letters on the bottom right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Could we focus in on the bottom right part of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And zoom in a bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Once you've read that, Mr. Vukovic, could you tell us if that informs you about what the straight lines on the map might represent?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: These straight lines might represent radio-relay routes between command posts of certain units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could I ask the Registrar to move west on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this is related to BH Army or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot really interpret this map. I did not draft it, nor did anyone from my centre produce this. This map is totally new to me and unfamiliar. But from what I see, I can tell that it's a diagram of communications between some centres of communications and commands of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps could I ask the Registrar to move to the west, and we'll see there something which might assist you in determining which army this relates to. If we could focus in a little bit on the central part there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does that help you at all, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: From what I see before me, I can assume -- unless this was produced by someone from the other side, the other party, the other armed forces, the BH Army, I can assume that this was perhaps developed within units of the Main Staff of the VRS. However, the map that you're showing me here could also have been produced from the communications -- from a communications unit of the BH Army. It could also be a VRS map. This is the first time that I see this map, and I'm not really competent to interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Vukovic, do you accept that it appears to denote a curled line going from Veliki Zep to Han Pijesak, as in the earlier Drina Corps map that you inspected?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, based on this code-name, "Panorama," "Panorama" or "Prostor," space, I can tell that this is a VRS map, and the curled line would then denote a wire line between Han Pijesak and the radio-relay node at Veliki Zep. But, again, I'm not competent to interpret this map. However, I do see that, based on what I see before me, that this was a map developed at the Main Staff of the VRS. I judge that by this code-name, "Panorama."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we can look further down the map, just further south, we see a straight line, and it ends with the word "Pale." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you express what that straight line might refer to?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This line, according to me, is a radio-relay route between Pale and Veliki Zep, but that would have had to go through Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. Your Honours, we'll be showing this particular map to other witnesses, who will be familiar with it. Nevertheless, I believe Mr. Vukovic has provided some useful information about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Vukovic, you referred to "Panorama" as a code-name. It's a code-name of which organ, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the Communications Centre at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So "Panorama" was the code-name for the Communications Centre of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections? We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2798, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, subject to the tendering of those associated exhibits which have not already been admitted by the Trial Chamber, that ends my examination-in-chief. So I'd like to tender the balance of the exhibits at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have any objections to any of them, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted just one typo, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. I meant to clarify one thing, Mr. President. I sent an e-mail to the parties and to the Trial Chamber about that. The exhibits that we're tendering are all of those referred to in the amalgamated statement, itself. Now, in the appendix which we filed with our 92 ter notification, we omitted six 92 ter numbers which are, in fact, discussed by the witness in his statement. I can read those into the record at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The six 92 ter numbers which were not listed in Appendix A, but which are discussed by the witness in his amalgamated statement, are 18575, 17569, 18577, 22866, 21272, 22909. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said 92 ter numbers? 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. 65 ter numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In your second-last item in the first page, you refer to 65 ter 13606. Is it not a typo for "13626"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, that's very possibly the case. I'll verify that. Unless I come back to you, that is the understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit them all. The Court Deputy will assign appropriate numbers and inform the parties. Thank you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, if you are ready, start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I didn't have an opportunity to meet you before you began your evidence here, but I would like to thank you for meeting my associates, and I hope that our cross-examination will run more smoothly and more quickly as a result.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major -- I would now like to request that we move briefly into private session or a closed session because of a bit of information that my Defence has obtained, and I need to be in private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, when Mr. President asked you to explain the part that the interpreters didn't catch, you explained what your role was. And it was thanks to that role of yours that you knew what the location of various installations was about the town?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked before the war, and it was TO 2120 Sarajevo that was my superior command, and Velesici came under that particular command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to this particular feature, do you recall any other military installations being present in Velesici?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a training centre in Velesici which specialised in training senior officers of the Territorial Defence in the former Yugoslavia. They were members of town TO staffs. There was also an arms depot there, as was a general storage place for military equipment. All of this was housed in the facility at Velesici, which is located just next to the General Motor Car Servicing Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was this particular General Motor Car Servicing Centre that serviced and repaired military vehicles before the war?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of this. We had our observation posts at various points in the town, and VRS personnel observe the movement of enemy personnel and their equipment, especially those that posed a threat to our forces, our commands, and various military and civilian authorities. They reported to us whenever such movement was observed. Our duty, among other things, was to protect the civilians from surprise attacks, including artillery attacks, aircraft raids, or sabotage actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there a hotel facility belonging to the railways or something of the sort there, and was the Delta Unit stationed there or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where the Delta Unit was stationed. It was a special sort of unit. I did hear of it, as I heard of the Black Swans. However, there was the secondary school for railway staff stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, sir, before the war broke out, you had the Municipal Centre for Monitoring and Reporting at Pale, and the capacities you had were those required by a municipal centre of this sort; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the monitoring and reporting activities intended for civilians, can you confirm or deny that Pale were also the subject -- was also the subject of mortar and howitzer fire?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to our duties related to encryption, we were also duty-bound to monitor the activities in the air and on the land, especially when it came to combat activities directed against civilians and civilian authorities or VRS military installations. I do recall that back in 1992 - it was in the month of August - on around the 7th of August, 1992, the urban core of Pale came under artillery fire from the direction of Precko Polje, Cakre [phoen], which is between Bjelasnica and Mount Igman. It was at this time that the attack resulted in one death. It was a man I knew before the war, a resident of Pale. I don't know if I should mention his name or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that we owe him that much.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's late Njegos Marinkovic, who was killed on his own land, close to his home. He was on his way to the cattle barn. The shell landed on this out-building, and the shrapnel killed him. It was up until the 20th of August, 1992, that the artillery fire continued, when a 152-millimetre Nora ^ gun was finally detected. It was the gun that kept firing on the urban core, and it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, at page 14, in 1D3616 - we don't have to call it up; it's there for everyone to see - you explained what it was that the Republican Centre engaged in; i.e., encryption of data, monitoring and reporting. And at page 15 of that same testimony, you said that you served the municipal authorities and their needs. And now I will continue in English. [In English] "And due to a lack of men, we had the role of Republic centre, Regional Centre, and Municipal Centre, of the cryptographic data-protection system, and of monitoring and information." [Interpretation] As you grew out from a municipal centre into a republican centre, did you find yourself in difficulties with regard to personnel and equipment?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: May I just supplement what I said in that earlier testimony, when we talked about the artillery fire directed at Pale. There is this one detail that I left out, and if this honourable Chamber would allow me to explain this, I will move on to the evolution from the Municipal to the Republican Centre. I forgot to mention: The artillery fire that was also present in 1995, in the period between, I think, the 10th of June, 1995, and the 28th of July, 1995, there was non-stop fire. At a later date, on the 30th of August, 1995, there was an all-out attack across Republika Srpska, where VRS installations were targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I then ask you: The shelling of Pale between the 10th of June and the 28th of July, does it coincide with a major Muslim offensive on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We were able to observe, when Pale was shelled, since it was our duty to find refuge for civilians and to alert the civilian and military authorities of the threat coming from the enemy side, we were able to observe that as soon as aircraft appeared in the air, an alarm would be sounded in the enemy section of Sarajevo, where the civilian population would go into the shelters, and we would then come under attack. I'm sorry, should I clarify something?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm just waiting for the interpretation to end. Can you tell us, this Municipal Centre, as it grew into a republican centre which had more duties on its hands, did it come across difficulties, in terms of personnel and equipment that they had?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a municipal centre which had a small number of staff, because it had been set up for peacetime activities, which now had to transform into a republican centre and service the entire republic. We were confronted with a vast number of problems. In fact, the same number of staff we had in 1992, as we set about these activities, remained there on the 21st -- up until the 21st of November, 1995, at which point, in fact, the staff was downsized. Throughout this time, we had some eight to nine staff, including late Milorad Kotlica, who died in Nis in 1994 and was buried at Bonn [phoen], in Montenegro. He was in charge of communications and encryption. And we didn't have proper personnel to replace him there, so it fell upon me to take up these duties. We had very few people, we had very little equipment and assets that we were at great pains to maintain, and we were confronted with major problems. This was a period of time when communications systems worked intermittently because of the combat activities or because, simply, we had some of the wires crossing enemy territory. The enemy would engage in sabotage activities, cut these wires. They electronically surveilled our activities. They jammed our radio-relay communications across various routes and at various nodes. For this reason, the 67th Regiment that I mentioned provided great assistance to us in overcoming difficulties that we faced in these poorly-functioning communications systems. The MUP Communications Centre - I believe I mentioned this - had great difficulties at Pale. The chief of the Communications Centre was late Milenko Paunovic, also known as Mile, a friend of mine, who frequently complained to me about the difficulties he had or inability to carry out some of the difficulties where we were supposed to lend them a hand, and we did whenever we were able to. This does not mean that we were always able to assist him in whatever difficulties he had. There was many an occasion when he would not ask for our help at all. Of course, the Communications Centre I'm referring to belonged to the MUP, and the army had its own Communications Centre. I don't know if I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can we call up 1D3617 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the war, as part of your duties, you helped the Red Cross and various humanitarian organisations, including the UNHCR which, back in 1991, had to receive refugees from Western Slavonia, et cetera. Did this situation prevail during the war as well?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, it was a large influx of refugees from the former Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, from Western and Eastern Slavonia, from Bila Gora, Papuk, Okucani, and those areas inhabited by Serbs. Since there was an offensive by the Croatian forces, the population had to flee in 1991, and a number of those refugees came to Pale. We were helping those people set up communications amongst themselves. There were a lot of problems. Families were separated, parents and children, and they had spread out all the way from Krajina to Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the following page of this document. Can we look at the bottom of the next page. We're looking there -- we will see the information that the witness has just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement, is this your signature, and are you explaining here what was done, just as you have told us now? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Major. Can we tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1372, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you spoke about similar issues in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case in page -- 1D36136, on page 23, and then on page 31 you said that -- I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "We had our own problems. Those were the first months of combat operations, and those communications systems would be down quite often."

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now call up D95, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, do you recognise this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you agree, I am instructing the presidents of municipalities here in all villages in which the Croatian and Muslim inhabitants have handed over their weapons and do not intend to fight, should enjoy protection. Anyway, I would like you to look at the municipalities listed, where it says "Gorazde, by radio"; "Foca, by radio relay"; "Han Pijesak, by telephone"; "Sokolac, by teleprinter"; "Rogatica, by radio"; "Visegrad, by radio"; "Rudo, by radio relay to Foca and then by radio"; "Cajnice, by radio relay." Now, are you able to tell us why there is such an uneven method of communication and why was this not done with a single means?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We had problems, especially in this period from April 1992 throughout the rest of 1992, when certain communication routes were disrupted, certain types of communications were down. Since there was a small number of people available, we tried to fulfill all of our obligations in order to protect any citizen of the then Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina because at the beginning of the war, I think it was the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of the ethnicity, regardless of their place of residence, where they were located, and in this way we were trying to resolve the problem of communication. Telephones were not functioning, teleprinter communications were down, so we had to find a way to see what kind of communication could serve a particular type of area to reach a certain municipality, a centre, in order to be able to convey the users' dispatches, telegrams and orders. I know that there was the matter of protection for the Muslim and Croat citizens who had handed over their weapons, who did not intend to put up any kind of fight against the Army of Republika Srpska, and I recall very well that it was ordered that all those citizens had to be protected and looked after, offered the full extent of the protection of the Bosnian Serb Republic. I can see that in Gorazde, we used the -- we delivered the telegram by radio. Rogatica, also in Visegrad, the dispatch was delivered by radio. This was an ultrashortwave 745 or 700Y device which any ham radio operator would be able to use, and this is the type of communications that we managed to set up. And we managed to dispatch the telegrams to certain centres 24 hours a day, from where they were passed on further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. Do you see that the late Colonel Kotlica is suggesting here to me, because it will be copied to me, that I should inform the media. Does that indicate that he wasn't sure that all of that would go through and that it would be a better thing to also publish it in the media?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Very often, we didn't have return information, whether something reached its destination or not; for example, telegrams that were sent by ultrashortwave operators, by radio. We would receive a confirmation that it was received, but we don't know whether the same thing applied in Rogatica, in Foca, or in some other place where there was a communication centre. We were unable to know what was done there from Pale. They would confirm receipt, but we don't know whether the telegram was actually delivered or not. This is something that would perhaps need to be looked into.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I would like us to briefly look at P2412. Can we look at that in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: By establishment, you were under the Ministry of Defence before the war and during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise this telegram, and did you dispatch it to Banja Luka, all the bodies in the ARK and the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this telegram was sent. It was received in the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly at 0959 hours. I can see the number here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "1/92," is that the first telegram of some Serbian defence organisation?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the number from the log-book of outgoing telegrams. I don't have the log-book in front of me now, but that should be the number from the log-book. I can see at the top this number "45100 Banja Luka Municipal Assembly." That should have been the regional centre which was in Banja Luka at the time which received the telegram by teleprinter which was addressed to the governments of the autonomous region and the Serbian Autonomous Region of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to all Serbian assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All Serbian assemblies. Now, I would like to ask you to help us a little bit, in view of the fact that you're a member of the military. Are you familiar, and I assume that you are, with the Law on All People's Defence, and do you agree that pursuant to that law, every municipality had a sovereign right to defence on its own territory?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did have the right to defend its territory and endangered population from any type of enemy actions which endangered the civilian population or buildings on the territory of any of those socio-political communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it states in the first point the Territorial Defence was being formed? Would you agree that that would then mean that the municipal TOs were all being merged at the level of the Republic of the Serb -- of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they would be under the command of municipal, district, and regional staffs, and the republican staff of the TO?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is natural that all municipalities had their own TO. This was something that was true at the level of the whole of the former Yugoslavia, and at the level of the former republics making up the former Yugoslavia. The republics had their own municipal TO units, which would then break down to units in the municipalities. There were TO peacetime and wartime units. And they would break down into staffs. They had the required number of people available, and they functioned in peacetime. During war, military conscripts were called up, and they were deployed to TO units at different levels and strengths, and the units were commanded by non-commissioned officers who were in the commands of the TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, sir, in view of the fact that you were in the TO of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war, and that on the 16th of April, 1992, this is the first telegram of the Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, before that did the Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina have any type of armed formation?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, the Serbian side didn't have any formations, it didn't form any formations. But, for example, in 1991, I know that units were formed of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League already in Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were units that were formed by the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, sir, you were asked in the Zupljanin case, Stanisic/Zupljanin case -- this is 1D3616, page 21. They asked you if this document was passed down to the municipalities, and now I'm going to read what you said in English: [In English] "At the top of the document, you can see that the memorandum was in the centre in Banja Luka. And as far as I can remember, the number indicated on the document was the number of the fax in the Banja Luka centre. I can't tell you whether the operator faxed these documents to somebody else. I don't know that. I am not able to see it from the document without the log-book. If I saw the log-book, I would be able to tell you who the document was sent to. Since Banja Luka was a regional centre at the time and this document applied to all Serbian municipalities, I suppose that he did fax these documents to the municipalities in the Krajina region."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "And that's what I conclude based just on looking at the document." [Interpretation] So you know that there was possibly return information, that it did reach that centre, but what happened with this and similar documents is something that you cannot know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because I see here that the telegram was sent by teleprinter. In the memo of the telegram at the top, you can see that this was sent by fax, and there is a fax "12566." This is the Regional Centre in Banja Luka. So the Regional Centre in Banja Luka, unable to send it to all the municipalities by teleprinter because it was probably down, they sent the telegram by fax, which was not permitted. But at the time, that was how they did it because there was no other way to do it, and that means that a fax like this and a telegram like this, whoever was involved in anti-electronic surveillance could have been recorded. The tapping -- surveillance Centre could have picked up this document. It was not permitted to send text like this by fax because that was an open communication. If it was a protected document, and in this way, if it was sent, it would practically become a public one. Anyone could pick it up and record it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, in paragraph 46 of your statement, you say that by June there was no developed system of protection of military data and there was no encryption in order to protect data; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Encryption in our centre, i.e., Cryptographic Protection, began to operate, I think, around the 20th or the 22nd of June, so it was in the second half of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the same thing during your testimony in Stanisic/Zupljanin, 1D3616, on pages 59 and 60. Now, do you remember, Major, sir, that on the 20th of June, or maybe the 22nd, but I believe it was the 20th, the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian Muslim part, declared war on us?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of June, 1992, I believe, I believe that war was declared -- well, I believe that war was declared on the Republika Srpska far sooner. I believe there was an order of April 1992, consisting of four points, which arrived on the 29th of April, 1992, an order that was signed by the first commander of the so-called BH Army, because the Territorial Defence was just one component of the armed forces, the component of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. However, by issuing that order, consisting of four points, they declared war on the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I think that the authors of that order are still at large and that no one was ever brought to justice, not one of them, although all the following events -- the subsequent events, all the deaths and the suffering of the civilians, the Vase Miskina incident, the Markale I and II incidents, all of that arose from that first order, a monstrous order, because that order made it binding on every soldier of Bosnia and Herzegovina to wage war. This can also be -- this is also confirmed in a book issued -- published by Hasan Efendic, the first commander of the BH Army, the book entitled "Who Defended Bosnia." This book was published in 1991 by the Association of Noble Descent -- of People of Noble Descent in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this very order is mentioned on pages 135 or 136, or perhaps on the pages between 128 and 136, where Colonel Efendic makes a reference to that order of the 23rd of April, 1992, and says that that order had created a major disturbance both at Pale and in Belgrade. This order of 29th -- we received it on the 29th of April, 1992, at Pale. This was sent to all municipalities, this order, and they probably felt that Pale, too, would respond to this order and implement the four items listed there. And one such copy of that order was also handed in to you and the then Colonel Subotic. Another copy of this same order also arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I appreciate your detailed explanation, however we have only a limited time, so if you could concentrate on answering the question. So Mr. Karadzic will lead you with his questions. The question was whether Croatia declared war. Continue with your next question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly see D332, please, and see whether this is the document that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But my question was whether the formal declaration of war came on the 20th of June, 1992, and we were declared the enemy, "we," as Yugoslavia. First of all, is this the document that you're referring to, the document that was a trigger for war even before it was declared?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is that document of the 29th of April, 1992. That's the document I was just referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that there was an order on combat readiness that was issued by this same colonel on the 12th of April, 1992, and it preceded this order we have before us?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that document. I cannot recall it as I sit here. But I do remember this order, and I just mentioned it a moment ago, because it says in paragraph 4: "Hurriedly plan and begin combat operations in the entire territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and co-ordinate them with the territorial defence staffs of regions, districts and the Republic of BH." Practically, in paragraph 4, he is ordering that war should be waged on the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and each soldier of the BH Army had to enforce this order. And this is the source of all the problems in Bosnia and Herzegovina later on, and I find it hard to believe to this day that not one of the authors of this order ever were called to justice. It is really mind-boggling, and I don't know when Croatia did that. I don't know what that relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe the interpretation was incorrect. I said the Bosnian and -- Bosnian Muslim and Croatian part of the Presidency declared war.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. What I received as my interpretation was that it was Croatia, which I cannot confirm. But, yes, that the part of the Presidency consisting of the Bosnian and Croatian representatives did, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you just reminded me of another problem with Colonel Efendic. Could we now see 1D3618 in e-court, please. This is an interview that you had with the Prosecution. The Prosecutor interviewed you on the 27th of January, 2010. Could we see that, please, 1D3618. We need page 64 of the interview. Major, sir, do you remember what kind of measures were taken, and how strict was the enforcement, if a soldier would waste a single bullet in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was taken very seriously because each bullet meant a human life, so all the bullets, all the rounds that were issued, had to be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, here we see, and perhaps you can just glance at it - we're not going to read it out - but there is mention here of Territorial Defence of Sarajevo, and Hasan Efendic was part of it, and then you go on to say that somehow 40.000 rounds went missing, and then that Budimir Djordjic the prosecutor, tried to initiate the procedure in 1987 [Realtime transcript read in error "1997"] or 1988 [Realtime transcript read in error "1998"], but that he was not able to continue with it, and that it was never explained and it was never clarified how it came about; correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was this issue where ammunition went missing from the depot at Koran?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would this 40.000 rounds approximately equate to 240 combat kits?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, because a lot of ammunition went missing then, and it was even reported in the press, in "Oslobodjenje," because there was a clash within the Territorial Defence Staff. And I know this because at the time I was the deputy -- I was the assistant commander for mobilisation and recruitment in Pale, and I was also involved in security and intelligence. And the assistant commander for logistics complained to me that he could not account for that amount of ammunition and a certain number of long barrels, and then it was said that that was not quite the case. I even happened to fall ill at the time. I got blood poisoning, I ended up in hospital, so that's where it remained. But I know that they tried to clarify this, but the military prosecutor who tried to conduct an investigation, he did manage to identify where the problem was. He was preparing to issue an indictment against the individuals who are responsible for this. However, this indictment was never issued, probably because of the clash that ensued, and this same person later on became one of the first commanders of the BH Army. And then we know what happened next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to point out an error in the transcript, just in case it isn't picked up later. The events we're looking at took place in 1987 or 1988, not 1997 and 1998, which brings me on to my second point. In my submission, this entire area of evidence is really of very little assistance to the Chamber, concerning, as it does, events five years before the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I reply to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect for Mr. Gaynor, this gentleman, Efendic, he was the commander, the man responsible -- the responsible man at the time of this theft. On the 11th of April, he became the commander of the Territorial Defence, and on the 12th of April, he ordered attacks. On the 29th of April, he ordered an all-out attack. And this theft of ammunition was, in fact, to benefit his side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We still have a question how relevant this is to your case. Come to the question which is relevant to your case and to the issues he dealt with in his examination-in-chief. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that up until mid-June, approximately, or, rather, at the declaration of war, there was no code for protecting military data. And then in paragraph 9 of your statement, you said that at that time a code system was established, and it was referred to as "Vatra" or "Fire." Could you tell us how that came about and how the whole thing functioned?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of June, 1992, at the Republican Centre of Communications, we established a code system to encode communications that were going out to certain addressees. Now, the communications plan, code-named Vatra, was a communications plan for maintaining radio communications, so it is a code-name for radio communications, where radio units -- radio sets were used, and it did not contain only one code book, but a number of code books and documents, such as identifying documents, the code book, then the key for the code book. So, in other words, this is a communications plan for the secret commanding of troops, or TKT for short. This Vatra plan of communications could also be applied for telephone communications and it would then -- it could then be forwarded to the addressees or the end users either by telephone lines or through the radio communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, today, during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned that -- on page 51, line 11, that services developed their own documents independently. Would you please tell the Trial Chamber what you mean by the word "documents"?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, "documents," that means those are parts of a communications plan. So, for instance, the communications plan code-named Vatra consisted of a number of documents, such as the keys for the codes, and the communications plan code-named Vatra consisted of a code book. And at a certain point in time, that communications plan was called Vatra. Some, say, 10 months later or 15 months later, the code-name would change to, for instance, Apollo. Then some few months later, it would be renamed and called Ares. So all these were code-names for the plan. The plan, itself, contained keys. For instance, the plan would have Lines A and B, and then there would follow five-digit numbers that would, in fact, be the keys to the code book. And then, in alphabetical order, there would be different terms that are developed in the code book, itself. For instance, if there was an aircraft in question, then there would be a five-digit number that would, in fact, stand for the word "aircraft"; for instance, that an aircraft was observed or used in an area and so on. So this plan could be used for communicating covertly. In other words, that was the plan for the secret commanding of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that various services would each develop their own documents, and you mentioned a moment ago that after some time those documents would have to be changed, is it correct that such documents at times had to be sent by courier to the end user so that they could all change the code-name at the same time or the whole code at the same time, and that this was a timely and risky endeavour?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, because they all had to reach certain centres at the same time, I mean the changes in the plans. This would be done via radio, for instance, where a special frequency would be agreed, and then they would relay the information about where such code books and plans should be taken over. And then couriers would take them to these locations at the time, the agreed time, and they would take them over and take them to the centres where they were to be used. Now, this, of course, was a very timely project. Now, all of the various services developed their own plans, their own systems. The police had its own and the army had its own, and they were independent of each other, and they developed their own documents as part of their radio communications systems. However, we could exchange the documents amongst ourselves. And if it was necessary, if all our communication lines were down, we could try and use those plans in order to establish the communication, pending the repairs of our downed communications lines or system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, sir, you prompted me to ask you that in paragraph 28 of the amalgamated statement, you spoke about these stationary nodes, Jahorina, Veliki Zep and so on, radio-relay connections. Even though each of you had your own documents, did you share the difficulties you all encountered when there would be a power cut, when the fuel would run out for the generators, when combat would be directed at radio-relay facilities on the hills, and at other times? Did this equally affect all the services, the police, the military and the ministry?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at it from my own point of view, and based on the experiences in combat, let's say, during the bombing of facilities at Jahorina, the VRS communications system was damaged. It was difficult to set up communications between the Main Staff and the units, so then we activated our own system of communications using our centres, and thus we managed to receive information from certain areas. For example, this was in 1995 when there was an offensive on the Western Krajina, when the VRS communications system was destroyed, when the Jahorina facilities were ripped up from the ground, practically, when the communications were broken down, when it was very difficult to carry out repairs and maintenance. We used radio communications developed by the Republican Centre for Monitoring Information, Communications, and Cryptographic Data protection from Pale. So through this, we managed to convey brief information to and from the Main Staff, because they could not use their own communication links to be able to report back and forth about everything that was happening on the ground. It was very difficult to set up communications. The police also had their own communications system, which I cannot comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that also depended on the status of the relays. Other than the radio-relay communications, how much did the other types of communication depend on the PTT system?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in quite a lot of cases, they depended a lot on the PTT system of communications, but even that was damaged, because they also used those repeaters, those relays, to maintain the communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told the Defence how, from time to time because of difficulties and lack of equipment, you had to tie equipment to radiators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is true. At the beginning of combat activities, this happened at the MUP school at Vraca. The school was moved. It passed hands from the B and H MUP to the Republika Srpska MUP, and there was a communications centre there which was destroyed. And those people who were there, our police that was located in that centre, was unable to communicate with their superiors, their superior commands. Colonel Kotlica and I went downstairs and -- well, it's not an anecdote. Actually, it's our reality. Since they had some shortwave radios -- ultrashortwave radios, in order to set up any kind of communications, we tied those radio devices of theirs to the radiators, and then they served as antennas. So you can imagine how reliable and secure that kind of connection was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown document P2798 today, and the document has the heading, some sort of counter-electronic warfare. Is it correct that the 2nd Corps wire-tapped -- not only the 2nd Corps, but that it was also trying to listen in to our radio-relay communications? I'm talking about the Muslim army here.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was registered that they were involved in counter-intelligence activities and that they tried to wire-tap our communications. This is normal in all kinds of combat, that the enemy tries in any way possible to acquire data by wire-tapping or eavesdropping. Many times, we had the case of registering such events. The units that were supposed to create peace or implement peace were also involved with that, gathering information from specific units and so on, or about specific units. I cannot really interpret a map which I'm not familiar with. I saw it for the first time here a little bit earlier. I don't know what's there, what's what. I did not draft the map. I don't know when it was created, in which period. But I remember that at times when we were supposed to send you a telegram - I don't know if you were in your office or you were somewhere else, I don't remember - you didn't inform us about your movements, but I remember very well that Mr. Milanic, Gordan was a chief on your end at one time, and he informed me - this was summer 1995 - that you were going to be somewhere in Banja Luka, and that we tried to send a telegram to you through the 1st Krajina Corps, if we are not able to deliver it to your office in Pale. So I am not able to actually say what happened, because a lot of time has passed since then. I couldn't say where you were. I don't know if you were in the territory of Pale, or the territory of Banja Luka, or perhaps you were in Belgrade at the time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, sir, when you mentioned that, do you happen to remember that information to secure routes were routed through you? Do you remember that I travelled a lot all over the country and that I travelled a lot abroad for negotiations, peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and I remember when, for example, you had a peace conference in Lisbon, and Mr. Carrington was there, I think, at the time. The hydroelectric power-station in Visegrad was mined at the time, and you were supposed to fly from Belgrade to that peace conference at the time, and we managed, since there was the danger of the hydroelectric power-plant being knocked down by that Muslim side, the then Muslim side at the time, we managed to find an architect, the one who actually designed the station, Mr. - can I mention his name? - Dragan Bulajic. And so when you were just getting into the plane, we told you that you can fly freely, without any worries, there's no need to worry, that it was an insignificant amount of explosives, and that it could not really damage significantly the hydroelectric power-plant in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Well, about the protected radio-relay communications, you know that we have a whole collection here, that Croatia, itself -- not Croatian from Bosnia, but Croatia practically recorded every single word of ours that passed through that communication of ours?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is possible, probably because the Pleso Airport was also where the NATO had installed its own listening centres. We knew that they had a listening centre there, and all the hostile parties tried, by all possible means, to register all conversations by various methods. We had some devices or stations in our centres which could register anybody picking up any phone. These were some Alin stations. That was the model that operated on low frequencies, and it could register certain telephone conversations just like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I ask for D235 for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can I ask you to look, together with us, at what the situation was with the military communications in 1992. This is an analysis of combat readiness. Can we look at that document. That is document D325. No, no, that's not it. Either we made a mistake or -- combat readiness analysis. It's a different thing. All right, we have the correct document now, and let's just wait for the English version. Can we look at 27 in Serbian and page 30 in English, paragraph 1, please. Paragraph 1, I'm not sure if this the correct page. Yes, it should be. The first paragraph: "Combat missions in 1992 were characterised by frequent changes in the situation, continuous operations, heavy shelling of communications stations and centres, of stationary communications centres, stationary communications hubs, PTT communication centres, auxiliary PTT communications centres and connections, at a time of simultaneous and massive-scale offensive and defensive operations on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this something that comports with your information and experience?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible. I'm seeing this type of report for the first time, but it's all possible, it was possible. Certain nodes and hubs were the targets to be destroyed in order to prevent functioning and to damage the communication lines. Well, I'm not able to comment on the report. I did not participate in its drafting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the situation sounds familiar to you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is quite usual. There were actions like this; and there was a continuous threat to the nodes and the communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 4? I don't want to read it, but it says that the biggest problem was the destruction of the stationary section of the system, especially some vital objects like Bjelasnica, Zlovrh and Vlasic? Was this something that affected you as well, this loss of communications at Mounts Bjelasnica, Zlovrh and Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we had a lot of problems that we had to bridge by other communications, those problems. For example, we had a lot of problems in the functioning of the communications in the direction of Herzegovina, towards Trebinje, because the facility and node at Boracko Jezero, Orasnica [phoen], was problematic because it was unable to cover the whole area, so we had problems there and constant back-ups and hold-ups on the command-and-control line. There were plenty of problems there, not just at those three facilities at Bjelasnica, Zlovrh and Vlasic. There were problems at other places as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the following page in the Serbian. The English page can stay. Can we look at paragraph 6 in the English, and on the following page in the Serbian, can we look at paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with what it states here, that the situation was similar with others? Towards the bottom, there was similarities with other places, and it states that facilities at Ljuta, Konjic, Bosut, Trebevic, were damaged, and other facilities that were earlier in the communications system, these places were damaged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.
