utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs 3 and 4 say the same thing. On the English, page 31, let's look at paragraphs 1 and 2 from the top. You can see that on the Serbian page. Eleven facilities, out of a total of 32 facilities, 11 were left or destroyed, three were damaged, and there is a review also about that in the English version on page 31, paragraphs 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: These facilities were covered by the military, and it was their duty to compile reports of this kind. And these reports are quite realistic. As far as specific problems were concerned, they informed us, but they didn't inform us about all the problems; for example, problems at damaged facilities. There was time required for radio-relay communications or certain routes to be set up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 29, Serbian, paragraph 4, and English, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's completely the same situation with the VVF radio network which, at the very beginning, with the destruction of other communications, has completely been thrown out of the communications system. Can you please tell us what this WWF system is?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This is very high-frequency radio waves. We didn't have a system like that, this was a system that the army had, and these were the types of problems they were facing. I don't recall us working with the VVF communications at our centre.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at page 35 in the Serbian and page 39 in the English now. Last paragraph on the Serbian page, and in the English, page 39, paragraph 3, where it is also noted that there is lack of staff, senior officers at key posts, and it is noted that there are no radio-relay technicians, radio teleprinter operators, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this something that crippled the military as well and damaged its capability to communicate?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were problems like this throughout the whole 1992-1995 period, and it is precisely for these reasons that we were facing certain problems, shortage of staff with certain special skills; for example, radio technicians, radio-relay operators, radio teleprinter operators. There were problems, and because of that and because of what the army needed at the beginning, we talked about organising and the classification of posts in our system, from the regional to the municipal level. We organised all those three functions, the Municipal Centre, the Regional Centre and the Republican Centre, with the same number of people. That was eight people plus the odd colonel or the communications manager, who was the ninth man. But as I said, he died in 1994, so we were left with a set number of eight people who had to perform all the duties and tasks that were before us from 1992 to 1995. There was this shortage of staff in all the units, and this was a major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to briefly refer you to a portion of the interview of General Subotic. That's 65 ter 22622, page 3, please. I will read out a portion of his answer. That's toward the bottom of the page. Could we please yes, scroll it down. Thank you. [In English] "Yes, of course. Regular reports were sent. Regular reports. Practically daily reports. After the communications system were set up. I would say that that started in the beginning of 1993. Halfway through 1992 to the end of 1992, it was based on what was possible. But from 1993, we had communications between ..." And so on. [Interpretation] Do you agree with this statement of General Subotic, that from 1992 to the end of 1992, it was based on what was possible, but then in 1993, a communications system sort of became settled?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, basically we could take this to be a true description, because we were attached to the Ministry of Defence, and General Subotic was there at the beginning of the war as the minister of defence. We sent regular reports on the telegram and other traffic, which went through the regional and republican and municipal centres. And this is a very good observation, and I believe that he gave a pretty good picture here in his report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that Mr. Gaynor will need some time to put questions to you, so I will just have one final question -- or, rather, one final topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read everything that you sent, and did you read everything that came in to your centre?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Each operative who worked at the Communications Centre, especially at the encryption station, had to read and review what had arrived, and then to be -- and then to be aware if there was any interventions needed. But you know how it was. In our work, you had to forget what you had read out as soon as you've done it. So we didn't do any corrections or anything. We just returned documents to the senders. For instance, for us it was very important to have -- to know the exact log-books -- to keep the log-books very precisely so that those log-books would show each document coming in or going out; the time, date, and so on. However, there were a lot of documents in our log-books that were not only from our republic centre, where I was the chief of centre in 1995, and those log-books were not very up to date. There were a lot of omissions that I was able to observe. But whether the officers took any measures to improve the way records were kept, I don't know. But in any case, the information should be contained in the log-books as to who the document was sent by, who it was processed by, and whom it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you whether there was anything, in your knowledge, that was ordered or recommended or proposed and that would be against the law, in terms of the laws of war, anything. So was there ever any order that would not be in keeping with those laws and regulations?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as your orders or any written document coming from you, or orders or decisions coming from any of the commanders, irrespective of the level, all of these men were highly educated, and they were fully aware of the time and space where they were working and operating and what was going on, and I know that you always ordered that each individual, from the very last private up until to the highest officer, had to be aware of the laws on war and the Geneva Conventions in order to be able to act in keeping with them. And that was an order that was issued by you, and I know that at the centre where I worked as the chief of the service, I informed everyone, to the last officer, of the Geneva Conventions and all of its provisions, but particularly those that related to prisoners of war and the treatment of civilians. And as far as I can recall, I cannot remember any instance where you ordered anything that would be contrary to law and legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Major, for making the effort to come to The Hague to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any questions from you for re-examination, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Major, earlier on today you gave evidence that -- I'll read out a quote of what you said: "For example, this was in 1995, when there was an offensive on the Western Krajina, when the VRS communications system was destroyed, when the Jahorina facilities were ripped up from the ground, practically, when the communications were broken down, when it was very difficult to carry out repairs and maintenance." Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. This was in 1995, on the 30th of August, 1995, at 0155 hours, when the mass bombing of Republika Srpska began, and especially the bombing of a communications centre in Jahorina and Pale. So not only were they disrupted, the systems; they were ripped out of the ground. And when I say "ripped out," I mean with all the bombing, where very heavy bombs were used, they just came out of the ground. And all of these systems were disrupted. In Jahorina alone, we had 5 dead and 3 wounded soldiers. The entire facility was destroyed. People were practically blown out or blown away from the facility. We couldn't even recover their bodies. And as for the main relay centre at Jahorina, the so-called U-4 facility where there was Captain --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. It was the date of the incident that I was interested in, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would you expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Literally, about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If that could be provided. Yes. Could I call up, please, 23160.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you'll see this document in front of you, you'll see it's dated the 30th of August, 1995. And on the next page, we'll see it comes from General Mladic. And this, indeed, in the first paragraph, refers to what you've just described, if we go back to page 1. You just described the large-scale NATO attacks on the 30th of August. Can you just look at the first paragraph and tell me if this is what you were referring to? Could we -- thank you. If we could blow up paragraph 1, please, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a reference to that same incident, and I remember that I received a report from the Main Staff, from General Tolimir. I was advised that we might be targeted, that there was -- that we were one of the possible targets. And he also mentioned the possible time, 01, 03, 05, 07, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender that and just to show one other document. Could I have 23159, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2825, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next document is also dated the 30th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This document is not in your language, I'm afraid, Major, but it is from Janvier at UNPF in Zagreb to Annan at UN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do we have it in -- I beg your pardon. Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, on the first paragraph of this document, Major, you see a reference to NATO air-strikes, and it says they were predominantly targeted against the Bosnian Serb Integrated Air Defence System, that is, radar, missile and communications sites. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, is that also a reference to the attack that you were referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a reference to that, except that the attack started exactly at 0155 hours; not at 0210 hours, but it started exactly at 0155 hours on the 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to be aware of any co-ordinated NATO attack on Bosnian Serb communications targets prior to 30th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were air-strikes. For instance, there was an air-strike on the 25th and the 26th of May, 1995, in other words, some three to four months prior to this, and these were air-strikes on Pale, and some warehouses were destroyed at the Jahorinski Potok site, where the Depot 23 was destroyed. And a private was lightly wounded at the time, but there was a lot of material damage. This was an air-strike on the 25th. There were six aircraft which participated in the attack, in the air-strike. The aircraft were A-10 Thunderbolt and F-16. And on the 26th, there were 14 air-strikes, also targeting Jahorinski Potok and destroying several ammunition depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I interrupt there just so --

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- we can get through this as soon as possible. Though air-strikes, can you confirm, to the best of your knowledge, they were targeting ammunition dumps or depots, as you've just said?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: These air-strikes of the 25th and 26th targeted also ammunition dumps. However, before they destroyed the ammunition dumps, it would be necessary - and this would be in any army - to destroy anti-aircraft defence facilities. And in order to do that, you also have to destroy communications centres and nodes because it is necessary to disrupt the command-and-control chain. And the forces that carried out these air-strikes, they carried out air-strikes of these facilities on the ground, but they also protected the air-space from any other flights. However, they did not accomplish what they were supposed to, but they did bomb and carry out air-strikes on any facility that could present a threat to them. So they did conduct air-strikes on communications centres; for instance, on Jahorina, where there was a communications centre for the Main Staff which had links to the other units in that territory, because I remember that when that was accomplished, they flew at a lower height, altitude, and they just sort of waved their wings and flew away. Mr. Gaynor, I thank you for treating me fairly, and I thank you for having understanding for me, but you will understand that I am kind of eager to get home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I think I'll just end with this, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The air-strikes targeting the ammunition dumps in Pale have been the subject of evidence before Their Honours already in this trial. Are you suggesting that there was an attack on Bosnian Serb military communications facilities prior to the May attack, similar to the one which started on the 30th of August, 1995, or could it be that you're thinking of the one that started on the 30th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RANKO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, any attack against any target requires very careful preparation and protection of one's own forces from strikes from the other party. Now, I remember this attack of the 25th of May, 1995, which, during the first air-strike on the Jahorinski Potok Barracks, that attack started sometime at around 1550 hours, around 4.00 p.m., in other words, and there were six aircraft that participated, that took part in that attack. They were F-16 aircraft. And on that occasion, the Ammunition Dump 23 was destroyed, and one soldier was slightly wounded. However, when you have a synchronised attack against such facilities, you also have to ensure that there is radio communications and electronic jamming to disable the anti-aircraft defence system. On the 26th of May, there were 14 formations that took part in the air-strike on Jahorinski Potok, and as a man who was at the Centre for Monitoring and Information, I monitored all the information through my own system regarding the situation in air-space on that territory. And we registered 14 formations that carried out sorties against 26 facilities in Jahorinski Potok.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: On the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a problem with these facilities at Jahorina because, in addition to a radar installation that was monitoring the air-space between the Mediterranean Sea and the territory of Yugoslavia, the thing is they had to disable those radars as well. There was strong jamming and also some targeting of those antenna systems and radar installations. And as soon as that happened, as soon as you targeted those facilities, immediately you would disrupt the communications system. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender the cable from Janvier to Annan of the 30th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2826. And by hearing nothing from you, Mr. Tieger, I take it that there's nothing to be added to what is contained in your written response about the disclosure violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you were. When you indicated the end of the day, we are preparing a written submission which will be filed by close of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. That concludes your evidence, and on behalf of the Tribunal and the Bench, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I thank the Tribunal, and also the Prosecution, as well as the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd also like to extend my thanks to the staff members for their patience. Tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.41 p.m.,
